note: Every rule in this pack (titles, bodies, and the numbers inside them -- resolution figures, thresholds, rules of thumb) was drafted by Claude from general microscopy practice, not sourced from a specific citation, and has not been reviewed by a microscopy specialist. Treat it as a starting point to check against your own protocol and instrument, the same posture web/kb/spectra.json's overlapRules note takes toward its own thresholds.

rules.title: STED bleaches far faster than confocal -- pick dyes for photostability, not brightness
rules.body: The depletion beam deposits far more energy per pixel than excitation alone, so a dye that looks bright on a confocal can bleach within a few STED frames. ATTO 647N and Abberior STAR dyes hold up; many Alexa dyes do not.

rules.title: Undersampling throws away the resolution STED is buying you
rules.body: STED resolution is roughly 30-80 nm depending on depletion power and dye, well below a typical confocal pixel size. If the pixel size isn't set to Nyquist-sample that resolution, the extra resolution never reaches the data.

rules.title: Mounting medium and coverslip thickness matter more for STED than for confocal
rules.body: A mismatched refractive index between the mounting medium and the objective's immersion oil introduces spherical aberration that visibly degrades STED resolution with depth. Use a high-RI, low-photobleaching mountant and a #1.5H coverslip with a high-NA oil objective.

rules.title: Opening the pinhole trades optical sectioning for signal -- state it deliberately
rules.body: The default pinhole size of 1 Airy Unit balances signal and out-of-focus light rejection. Opening it gathers more signal from a dim sample but lets in more out-of-focus blur, directly reducing your optical sectioning.

rules.title: Check your pixel size against Nyquist sampling before you commit to a design
rules.body: An undersampled pixel size throws away real optical resolution regardless of how good the objective is. The correct pixel size depends on numerical aperture and emission wavelength -- most acquisition software has a Nyquist calculator built in. If you set the smallest feature you need to resolve instead, the 'set your pixel size from the smallest feature' rule derives the same Nyquist pixel size from that feature size rather than from NA/wavelength -- treat the two as one decision viewed from different starting points, not two separate checks.

rules.title: Overlapping emission spectra need sequential scanning, not simultaneous
rules.body: Simultaneous multi-laser scanning is faster but lets bleed-through between channels with overlapping emission masquerade as real colocalization. This works for dyes that are separable by excitation; if excitation peaks are also close, scanning sequentially will not separate them and the excitation-proximity warning applies instead. If your markers' emission spectra overlap but their excitation peaks do not, scan sequentially, one laser line at a time.

rules.title: Widefield has no optical sectioning -- thick samples come out blurred
rules.body: Out-of-focus light from every plane in the sample reaches the detector at once, since there is no pinhole to reject it. For anything much thicker than a monolayer, plan on deconvolution afterwards or switch to confocal or spinning-disk.

rules.title: Widefield is often the RIGHT choice for dim or photosensitive live samples
rules.body: Confocal's laser scanning delivers a much higher instantaneous light dose per pixel than widefield's wide-field illumination. For dim, photosensitive, or fast live-cell work, widefield's lower phototoxicity and higher frame rate can outperform confocal despite the missing optical sectioning.

rules.title: Light-sheet imaging lives or dies on refractive-index matching
rules.body: A mismatch between the sample, the mounting medium, and the chamber liquid shows up as visible smearing or striping in the data, not a subtle loss of quality. Confirm your clearing or mounting protocol actually matches the refractive index your instrument expects.

rules.title: Light-sheet datasets are routinely hundreds of GB to TB per sample
rules.body: Multi-view and multi-timepoint acquisition at light-sheet speeds generates data volumes that catch people off guard. Plan storage and downstream compute (registration, fusion, deconvolution) before the acquisition, not after the disk fills up.

rules.title: Single-sided illumination casts shadow stripes behind absorbing structures
rules.body: Anything strongly absorbing or scattering in the light path (pigment, dense tissue, bubbles) casts a stripe artifact behind it when illuminated from one side. Dual-side illumination or pivot scanning removes most of it if your instrument supports either.

rules.title: For SEM/TEM, MARKERS means contrast agents, not fluorophores
rules.body: There is no fluorescence channel to name in electron microscopy. The MARKERS field is the right place for the contrast or staining agent instead -- uranyl acetate, osmium tetroxide, or immunogold, for example.

rules.title: SEM/TEM samples often don't have the usual biological/technical replicate structure
rules.body: Electron microscopy sample prep frequently produces one usable block or grid per condition rather than the parallel biological replicates a light-microscopy design assumes. Leave the replicate fields blank rather than forcing a count that doesn't reflect anything real.

rules.title: Conductive coating and section thickness shape image quality as much as the microscope does
rules.body: SEM charging artifacts trace back to coating thickness and conductivity, and TEM contrast and resolution trace back to section thickness. Both are easy to forget to note once you're looking at finished micrographs -- record them while prepping, not after.

rules.title: Raman is label-free, but that speed cost shows up in acquisition time
rules.body: There is no fluorophore panel to plan around, since Raman reads intrinsic vibrational signatures. In exchange, acquisition is slow -- seconds to minutes per spectrum or map point -- so scan area and point density become the real design tradeoff.

rules.title: Higher Raman laser power improves signal but risks local heating and sample damage
rules.body: A stronger signal-to-noise ratio comes at the cost of local heating, which can damage biological or otherwise photosensitive material well before it's visibly obvious. Start at low power, check for damage, and only raise it once you've confirmed the sample tolerates it.

rules.title: Set your pixel size from the smallest feature you need to resolve, not the other way around
rules.body: As a rule of thumb (not a strict requirement), sample at roughly 2 to 3 times finer than the smallest feature that matters -- Nyquist sampling. A common practical figure is about 2.3x the feature size, since the true optical resolution of a system is rarely known exactly at acquisition time. Undersampling throws away detail the optics can actually deliver; oversampling mostly costs storage and time. This is the same Nyquist pixel size confocal's own 'check your pixel size against Nyquist sampling' rule derives from numerical aperture and emission wavelength instead -- a feature-size estimate when you don't yet know your real resolving power, not a second, competing number.
